issues.subcategory: Incorrect sample-size arithmetic in computational analysis
issues.description: The manuscript states that 154 suffixes were identified, then says 64 suffixes were excluded and 95 remained. These numbers do not add up: 154 - 64 = 90, not 95. This undermines confidence in the corpus filtering and any reported means for the reduced suffix set.
issues.quote: This process revealed 154 written suffixes in total... In order to determine this, we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993).  For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.subcategory: Contradictory suffix inclusion threshold
issues.description: The Methods state that suffixes were extracted only if they occurred in at least three different words, yet Appendix A includes suffixes with type frequencies of 1 or 2. This contradicts the stated sampling frame and affects diagnosticity/specificity estimates, especially because rare suffixes are later discussed as highly diagnostic.
issues.quote: we extracted all spellings annotated as derivational suffixes in CELEX that occur in at least three different words.  This process revealed 154 written suffixes in total.

issues.subcategory: Appendix values violate stated inclusion criterion
issues.description: The appendix lists several suffixes with type frequency below three, inconsistent with the claim that only suffixes occurring in at least three words were included. Examples include +ante, +drome, +efy, +gen, +ison, +nik, +phone, +yse, and +yst. This matters because many corpus conclusions depend on rare suffixes and their perfect diagnosticity/specificity.
issues.quote: 31 | +drome | ... | Type frequency | 2 ... 34 | +efy | ... | Type frequency | 1 ... 109 | +nik | ... | Type frequency | 2 ... 153 | +yse | ... | Type frequency | 2

issues.subcategory: Incorrect specificity formula for token measure
issues.description: The token specificity definition appears to use the wrong denominator: it says summed frequency of all words that contain the spelling and fall into the category, which is essentially category-specific diagnosticity rather than specificity among all spellings of the sound sequence. Specificity should divide by the summed frequency of all words of that category with the relevant phonological sequence, regardless of spelling. If implemented as written, token specificity is not measuring the stated construct.
issues.quote: A second measure of specificity, based on word tokens, was obtained by dividing the summed frequency of words ending in this phonological and orthographic sequence and falling into this category by the summed frequency of all words that contain the spelling and fall into this category.

issues.subcategory: Lexical category treated as meaning without sufficient justification
issues.description: The central construct is framed as spelling-to-meaning regularity, but the operational outcome is lexical category. Lexical category is morphosyntactic, not semantic meaning in the ordinary sense. The manuscript cites a precedent but repeatedly generalizes to meaning, which risks construct overreach and misinterpretation of findings as semantic rather than grammatical-category sensitivity.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of “meaning”).

issues.subcategory: Morphological versus orthographic cue confounding
issues.description: The behavioral stimuli use suffix-like endings, but the experiments do not isolate morphological knowledge from sensitivity to orthographic ending statistics, phonotactics, or distributional regularities. The manuscript explicitly declines to include non-pseudoaffixed controls in Experiment 1, limiting claims that effects reflect morphological cues rather than broader orthographic cues.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.subcategory: No nonmorphological control endings in behavioral experiments
issues.description: Because no matched nonmorphological endings were used in the core experiments, the studies cannot determine whether participants rely specifically on derivational suffix knowledge. This is especially important because the paper makes strong claims about morphemes and suffix spellings being reserved for grammatical functions.
issues.quote: Using our linguistic analysis, we selected suffixes that are diagnostic for adjectives or nouns, and created nonwords ending in these suffixes

issues.subcategory: No baseline or neutral-context condition in spelling task
issues.description: Experiment 2 contrasts congruent versus incongruent sentence contexts, but lacks a neutral baseline. Without baseline spelling preferences, it is difficult to distinguish increased target spelling in congruent contexts from decreased use in incongruent contexts or from general spelling frequency biases.
issues.quote: For each suffix’s target spelling two context types were selected – one that was congruent with the category that this spelling denoted and one that was incongruent with it.

issues.subcategory: Context templates differ by lexical category and condition
issues.description: Sentence contexts differ systematically across noun, adjective, and verb conditions in syntactic structure, length, verbs, adverbs, and plausibility. Congruency effects may therefore reflect context-template differences, syntactic predictability, or semantic plausibility rather than suffix-category congruency alone.
issues.quote: Sixty-six sentences were designed following one of three possible context templates (noun, adjective, or verb template; see Table 4 for an example of each template). Nonwords in the noun context template occupied the syntactic position of a direct/indirect object following an adjective... Nonwords in adjective contexts appeared after verbs prove, stay, grow, smell... Nonwords in verb contexts followed an adverb.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete control of sentence materials in eye-tracking
issues.description: The pretarget region had significantly more words in the incongruent than congruent condition. Although the authors add an interaction term post hoc, this does not fully address potential differences in syntactic/semantic processing load, launch site distributions, or contextual predictability before the target.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous and potentially incorrect degrees of freedom for item matching test
issues.description: The eye-tracking matching test reports t(64), but the design appears to include 80 experimental nonwords or 120 sentences, with counterbalancing. It is unclear what units were tested and why df=64. This opacity prevents evaluation of the matching claim.
issues.quote: the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.subcategory: Incorrect comprehension accuracy reporting
issues.description: The manuscript reports average comprehension accuracy as 0.86%, with a range from 0.66% to 0.98%. These are clearly proportions (86%, 66%-98%), not percentages. This is a reporting error that can mislead readers about participant engagement.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent z statistic and p value
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the token analysis is reported as z = 0.60, p < 0.01. A z value of 0.60 corresponds to p around .55 in a two-tailed normal test, not p < .01. This is a clear statistical inconsistency affecting the claim that token specificity predicts spelling behavior.
issues.quote: for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01

issues.subcategory: Mislabelled model type
issues.description: The manuscript says specificity and its interaction were added to the 'linear model' for a binary dependent variable analyzed with generalized mixed modeling. This may be only a wording error, but it obscures whether the appropriate binomial GLMM was used.
issues.quote: we added the graded specificity metric for the target spelling to the linear model (values were different in different contexts because specificity of spellings was estimated relative to different categories), as well as its interaction with the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: Wrong chi-square notation for likelihood-ratio tests
issues.description: The likelihood-ratio tests are reported as Chi(2) rather than chi-square with 2 degrees of freedom, and in one case the model comparison description is unclear about exactly which terms were added. This is minor but reflects incomplete statistical reporting.
issues.quote: The addition of extra terms did not impact on the fit of the models (go-past times: Chi(2)  = 2.87, p > 0.2; regressions-out: Chi(2) = 0.23, p > 0.8)

issues.subcategory: Overinterpretation of non-significant trends
issues.description: The manuscript interprets p = .13 and p = .08 as trends supporting diagnosticity effects. These are not conventionally significant and should not be used as evidence without appropriate qualification, especially amid multiple exploratory tests.
issues.quote: whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13)... increased as diagnosticity increased in the incongruent condition (marginal significance, B = 0.21, z = 1.8, p = 0.08).

issues.subcategory: Multiple comparisons without correction or preregistered selection
issues.description: Experiment 3 tests multiple eye-movement outcomes plus diagnosticity interactions, but no correction for multiple testing or preregistered outcome hierarchy is reported. The authors state they monitored many measures because they had no concrete predictions, increasing false-positive risk.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: Exploratory outcome selection in eye-tracking
issues.description: The eye-tracking analysis involved many dependent measures and then emphasized those with significant congruency effects. Without preregistration or multiplicity control, this creates substantial analytic flexibility and selective emphasis concerns.
issues.quote: we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest, congruency... In sum, we found significant effects of congruency on go-past times and regressions made from the target nonword back to the preceding part of the sentence.

issues.subcategory: No preregistration reported
issues.description: The study reports OSF storage but does not indicate preregistration of hypotheses, sampling plans, exclusion criteria, model specifications, or primary outcomes. Given multiple experiments, many suffix metrics, and several alternative analyses, lack of preregistration increases concern about researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Data for all experiments can be found in the OSF storage for this project.

issues.subcategory: Post hoc exclusion rules in corpus analyses
issues.description: The General Discussion reports preliminary analyses that remove suffixes below certain diagnosticity/specificity thresholds and remove all suffixes with specificity/diagnosticity of 1. These exclusions are not preregistered or theoretically well justified, and they materially alter correlations with frequency.
issues.quote: For this analysis, we removed seven suffixes with diagnosticity below 0.35... Once we remove these 40 suffixes, a positive correlation is observed... As with the diagnosticity analyses, we excluded 20 suffixes with a low specificity... We also removed all suffixes with the specificity of 1

issues.subcategory: Entropy regression test is misinterpreted
issues.description: The regression slope of Hspelling on Hphonology is reported as significantly different from zero with t = 25.32, then separately different from 1 using F. The interpretation that slope < 1 means spelling is more predictive is not straightforward unless intercept and scaling are considered; comparing mean entropies or paired differences would be more direct. The reported mean difference is tiny (0.61 vs 0.63), and no effect size or paired test is provided.
issues.quote: A slope of 1 indicates that suffix pronunciations and their spellings provide the same degree of information about lexical category... We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01). That is, the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent entropy metric notation
issues.description: The entropy section alternates between Hsound, Hphonology, and H orthography/spelling without clearly defining whether the same variables are used. This weakens reproducibility of the analysis.
issues.quote: we calculated Hsound to provide an estimate of the prediction precision from the most frequent pronunciation of the suffix.  We then examined the slope of the regression equation lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology, weights = suffix frequency).

issues.subcategory: Random-effects structure likely underspecified
issues.description: The main GLMMs include only random intercepts for subjects and suffixes. The experimental manipulations vary within subjects and, in some cases, within suffixes/items, so random slopes for condition/diagnosticity should be considered to avoid anti-conservative fixed-effect tests. No justification is given for the simplified structure.
issues.quote: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject) + (1|suffix), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: Items/stems not modeled as random effects
issues.description: Behavioral experiments used nonword stems as stimuli, but models include random intercepts for subjects and suffixes only. Stem/nonword item variance is ignored, even though responses may depend on nonword-specific orthographic/phonological properties. This can inflate precision and reduce generalizability to new items.
issues.quote: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes.

issues.subcategory: Repeated suffix exposure and possible learning/strategy effects
issues.description: Participants saw multiple items with the same suffixes, especially in Experiments 2 and 3. This may induce explicit strategies or within-experiment learning rather than solely reflecting long-term knowledge. The authors mention list division in Experiment 1 but not adequate controls for learning across repeated suffix exposure in later experiments.
issues.quote: Each participant heard six nonwords containing each suffix: three times in a context congruent with the target spelling of the suffix, and three times in a context incongruent with it.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 conducted after unrelated session
issues.description: Experiment 1 was administered at the end of a longer unrelated testing session. Fatigue, carryover, or context effects from the prior session are not described or controlled, despite 11.7% missing/time-out responses.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.subcategory: High missingness in Experiment 1 not analyzed
issues.description: Experiment 1 excludes 11.7% of data due to timeouts or invalid button presses, but the distribution of missingness by condition, participant, suffix, or item is not reported. If missingness differs by suffix/category, estimates of response proportions and diagnosticity effects could be biased.
issues.quote: on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.subcategory: Unclear exclusion and missing data handling in Experiment 2
issues.description: Experiment 2 reports 1,914 analyzable data points, which equals 29 participants x 66 trials, implying no exclusions, but does not report whether any spellings were ambiguous, omitted, mistyped, or impossible to code. Manual suffix extraction without reliability reporting further complicates missing-data and coding evaluation.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points).

issues.subcategory: Eye-tracking exclusions incompletely reported
issues.description: The eye-tracking analysis discards 4% of trials after visual inspection, but exclusions are not broken down by condition, participant, or item. Because congruency effects could be biased if more noisy or incomplete trials occurred in one condition, condition-specific exclusion rates are needed.
issues.quote: All trials were also visually inspected in order to identify those where participants had not read the sentences in full, or where any considerable deviation in the eye-tracking trace was evident during the trial. As a result of these checks, 4% of trials were discarded.

issues.subcategory: Manual coding reliability absent
issues.description: Experiment 2 relies on manual extraction of suffix spellings from typed responses, but no coding rules, second coder, inter-rater reliability, or treatment of ambiguous spellings is reported. This limits replicability and raises potential bias in the dependent variable.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings

issues.subcategory: Insufficient participant demographic reporting
issues.description: The sample is described only as undergraduate native English speakers. Age, gender distribution, dialect background, handedness/vision for eye tracking, and literacy/spelling proficiency measures are not reported. These details are relevant for reading, spelling, and generalizability.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.  They were native English speakers with no history of reading, spelling, or learning difficulties.

issues.subcategory: No power analysis or precision justification
issues.description: No a priori power analysis, stopping rule, or sensitivity analysis is reported for any experiment. Sample sizes are modest, especially Experiment 2 with 29 participants and only 11 suffixes, making interaction tests and subgroup/suffix-level claims potentially underpowered.
issues.quote: Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London.  Sampling conditions were otherwise the same as in Experiment 1.

issues.subcategory: Underpowered suffix-level graded analyses
issues.description: The key claim that behavioral sensitivity mirrors graded diagnosticity/specificity is tested across relatively few suffixes: 20 suffixes in Experiments 1/3 and 11 in Experiment 2. Suffix-level correlations/interactions with so few units are unstable and vulnerable to leverage from individual suffixes.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected... Eleven suffix spellings that had a high specificity for noun, adjective, or verb lexical category were selected.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reporting of fixed-effect estimates and model details
issues.description: For several models, the manuscript does not report intercepts, coding schemes, confidence intervals, standard errors, exact p values, optimizer settings, distributional assumptions for transformed/continuous outcomes, or whether RT-like eye measures were transformed. This hinders evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes. However, in the interest of space we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest, congruency.

issues.subcategory: Untransformed skewed eye-movement times
issues.description: Eye-movement duration measures such as go-past time are typically skewed, but the manuscript appears to analyze raw millisecond values with linear mixed models. No transformation, residual diagnostics, or robust modeling is reported, potentially violating model assumptions and affecting inference.
issues.quote: This analysis considered the impact of congruency on the summed fixation duration (in ms)... There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.subcategory: Spoken nonwords recorded from IPA without acoustic control
issues.description: Experiment 2 uses auditory nonwords recorded from IPA transcriptions but provides no acoustic matching or verification of pronunciation, duration, stress, coarticulation, or intelligibility. Differences in auditory form could influence spellings independent of contextual category or suffix specificity.
issues.quote: The nonwords were pronounced by an adult female native speaker of British English and recorded in stereo at a sampling rate of 22,050 Hz. Items were presented to her in the IPA transcription format

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 target spelling may be driven by real-word analogy rather than specificity
issues.description: Although the authors argue no matching is required because the same phonological sequence appears in congruent and incongruent conditions, participants' spellings may be influenced by analogies to known words, base/stem plausibility, or suffix frequency. The design does not fully disentangle category-specific spelling from general analogy to real derivational forms.
issues.quote: Note that no matching was required, because the same phonological sequence was used in the congruent and incongruent conditions. Thus, any effect could not be attributed to the properties of the phonological sequence or its possible spellings

issues.subcategory: Potential mismatch between nonword syntactic contexts and claimed lexical categories
issues.description: Some contexts may not unambiguously impose the intended lexical category, especially adjective contexts after copular/perception verbs and verb contexts after adverbs. Some nonwords could be interpreted as adverbs, participles, or nouns depending on sentence semantics, undermining the intended manipulation.
issues.quote: Nonwords in adjective contexts appeared after verbs prove, stay, grow, smell, appear, taste, sound, seem, look, turn, become, remain, that maximised the probability that they would be perceived as adjectives. Nonwords in verb contexts followed an adverb.

issues.subcategory: No validation of sentence context category constraints
issues.description: The authors do not report norming studies showing that sentence frames strongly bias the intended noun/adjective/verb category or are matched for plausibility and predictability. This is central to interpreting congruency effects in spelling and eye tracking.
issues.quote: Sixty-six sentences were designed following one of three possible context templates (noun, adjective, or verb template; see Table 4 for an example of each template).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 filler verbs not analyzed despite being part of context distribution
issues.description: Verb-suffix fillers were included to vary contexts but not analyzed because most verb suffixes are not diagnostic. Yet their inclusion changes participants' expectations and task environment, and some verb fillers are congruent/incongruent. Excluding them may bias understanding of the full design and participant strategy.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be more varied. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category

issues.subcategory: Verb suffixes called diagnostic despite low diagnosticity rationale
issues.description: The manuscript says filler nonwords had suffix spellings diagnostic for verbs, then says the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category. This is internally inconsistent and obscures the role of verb materials.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added... These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 terminology error: adjective-specific instead of adjective-diagnostic
issues.description: The analysis of diagnosticity in Experiment 1 refers to adjective-specific suffixes, although the construct being tested is diagnosticity. This terminological inconsistency can confuse interpretation of feedforward versus feedback constructs.
issues.quote: observed the effect of diagnosticity on both adjective-specific suffixes (B = 4.5, z = 2.9, p < 0.01, i.e. highest absolute values for diagnosticity yield more adjective responses) and noun-diagnostic  suffixes

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 context labels conflict with table examples
issues.description: In Table 4, the incongruent example for the noun row uses '[dovate]' after an adjective in a noun syntactic position, but the table labels context as 'Noun'. The broader table structure may confuse whether 'Context' refers to syntactic context or suffix-target congruency. Clearer labeling is needed for replication.
issues.quote:
Context | Congruent | Incongruent
Noun | The candidate showed incredible [rabness] in a difficult situation. | The politician missed the urgent [dovate] after losing his phone.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect statement of English spelling-sound consistency
issues.description: The General Discussion says English letters map relatively consistently to sounds, which conflicts with the manuscript's repeated premise that English spelling-sound mapping is highly inconsistent/deep. This conceptual inconsistency weakens the framing of the argument.
issues.quote: English has an alphabetic writing system in which letters map relatively consistently to sounds.

issues.subcategory: Evolutionary causal claim not directly tested
issues.description: The manuscript suggests that English spelling evolved/fractionated to maximize meaningful information, but the main data are synchronic corpus and behavioral data. Diachronic mechanisms, selective pressures, and alternative historical explanations are not tested, so causal evolutionary claims should be framed more cautiously.
issues.quote: we close by arguing that English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.

issues.subcategory: Causal learning claims from adult correlational behavior
issues.description: The behavioral studies show adult sensitivity to suffix-category regularities, but do not demonstrate how this knowledge was acquired, whether implicitly learned, or whether it facilitates reading development. Claims about implicit statistical learning and lack of explicit instruction are plausible but not directly measured.
issues.quote: It is unlikely that our participants were ever taught these relationships explicitly; more likely is that this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes

issues.subcategory: Facilitation claim not fully supported by design
issues.description: The eye-tracking contrast shows processing difficulty for incongruent targets relative to congruent targets, but without a neutral baseline it cannot establish that congruent diagnostic spellings facilitate reading rather than incongruent spellings impairing it. The discussion makes both facilitation and disruption claims.
issues.quote: Reading is facilitated when suffix spellings that are strongly diagnostic of a particular lexical category are used in contexts that are congruent with that category; conversely, reading is disrupted when such spellings are used in contexts that are incongruent with that category.

issues.subcategory: Restricted participant population
issues.description: All participants are Royal Holloway undergraduates, likely young, educated, and literate British English readers. Findings may not generalize to children, less skilled readers, non-university adults, dyslexic readers, or speakers of other English dialects, yet claims are often framed as applying to skilled readers generally or the average reader.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.subcategory: English-only corpus and behavioral data overgeneralized to other orthographies
issues.description: The manuscript speculates that diagnosticity and specificity reflect general cognitive principles manifesting in other orthographies, but no cross-linguistic data are presented. Orthographies differ substantially in morphology, standardization, and phonology, so this claim is premature.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.subcategory: CELEX limitations not addressed
issues.description: The computational analysis relies on CELEX, an older database with specific lexical coverage and frequency estimates. The manuscript does not discuss how results might change with modern corpora, proper nouns, neologisms, dialectal variants, or contemporary spelling usage, limiting generalizability of corpus estimates.
issues.quote: We extracted all single-word entries from the CELEX database (Baayen, Piepenbrock & van Rijn, 1993), excluding any entries with spaces or hyphens.

issues.subcategory: Exclusion of non-major lexical categories biases diagnosticity/specificity
issues.description: The analysis considers only nouns, adjectives, and verbs while derivational suffixes may form adverbs, numerals, pronouns, or other categories. Appendix A contains suffixes with zeros across these categories or later excluded post hoc. This can inflate or distort diagnosticity/specificity and entropy estimates.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

issues.subcategory: Adverbs and -ly excluded/included inconsistently
issues.description: The corpus includes suffixes such as +ly and +ally but does not analyze adverb category, producing diagnosticity values near zero and entropy values that may be meaningless for the stated categories. This undermines claims about all English derivational suffixes.

issues.subcategory: Most frequent pronunciation only
issues.description: The specificity analysis uses only the most frequent pronunciation for each suffix. Many English suffix spellings have multiple pronunciations depending on word, stress, or dialect. Ignoring secondary pronunciations may misestimate specificity and phonological entropy.
issues.quote: Only the most frequent pronunciation was considered for each suffix.

issues.subcategory: Insufficient description of CELEX extraction algorithm
issues.description: The corpus extraction depends on identifying legitimate stems, pseudosuffixes, and alternations, but the precise algorithm, stem criteria, treatment of homographs, inflections, stress, pronunciations, and CELEX morphological annotation decisions are not fully specified in the manuscript. This makes replication difficult.
issues.quote: we extracted all words containing the spelling of each suffix, as long as the remaining (non-suffix) portion comprised a legitimate stem with at least one phonological vowel in the CELEX database (including stems with alternations i.e. orthographically conditioned variations, such as COMPLI-).

issues.subcategory: Pseudosuffix inclusion may conflate suffix knowledge with embedded letter-string statistics
issues.description: The corpus estimates include words where the suffix spelling does not function as a morpheme, motivated by morpho-orthographic segmentation evidence. However, this choice changes diagnosticity/specificity from properties of suffix morphemes to properties of terminal strings after valid stems, and may not align with the construct of derivational suffix knowledge.
issues.quote: However, in addition to extracting genuinely suffixed words, we also needed to capture words in which the suffix spellings do not function as genuine morphemes (e.g. the –ER in ‘corner’).

issues.subcategory: Computational conclusions stronger than data support
issues.description: The authors conclude that the majority of suffixes are diagnostic and specific, but the appendix includes many suffixes with low or undefined values for considered categories, and the mean is influenced by rare suffixes with values of 1. The manuscript later acknowledges low-value exclusions, creating tension with the broad conclusion.
issues.quote: Our analyses demonstrate that the majority of written English derivational suffixes are diagnostic and specific for some lexical category.

issues.subcategory: Misleading claim that fractionation cannot occur in transparent orthographies
issues.description: The claim that such fractionation could not occur in spelling-sound transparent writing systems is too strong. Transparent orthographies can still encode morphological or grammatical information through consistent morphemic spellings, diacritics, or morphophonological alternations. The assertion is conceptual overreach.
issues.quote: This fractionation could not occur in a spelling-sound transparent writing system.

issues.subcategory: Writing conveys more disambiguating information than speech overgeneralized
issues.description: The finding concerns written suffix spellings versus their most frequent phonological endings for lexical category. Speech contains prosody, stress, distributional context, and full word forms. Claiming the written signal conveys more disambiguating information than the spoken signal is broader than the analysis supports.
issues.quote: Second, it suggests that the written signal conveys more disambiguating information than the spoken signal in these cases.

issues.subcategory: No details on response-key counterbalancing
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses button presses for adjective/noun decisions but does not report key assignment or whether it was counterbalanced. Fixed mappings can create motor or response biases, especially in a two-choice classification task.
issues.quote: participants indicated their adjective-noun decisions via button press.

issues.subcategory: Timeout in unspeeded classification task may bias responses
issues.description: Instructions did not emphasize speed, but a two-second timeout was imposed, producing substantial missingness. This may disproportionately remove difficult or less diagnostic trials, biasing category-response estimates.
issues.quote: Instructions did not emphasise speed, although participants needed to make their decisions within a two-second timeout period.

issues.subcategory: No trial-order or fatigue effects reported for Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: Experiment 3 includes trial order in models, but comparable order/fatigue controls are not reported for Experiments 1 and 2 despite repeated suffix exposure and randomized presentation. This limits evaluation of practice or strategy development.
issues.quote: Experimental items were scrambled and presented in a different random order for each participant.

issues.subcategory: Diagnosticity threshold described as high despite including 0.50
issues.description: Experiment 1 states that all selected suffixes had high diagnosticity greater than or equal to .50. A value of .50 is chance-level for a binary noun/adjective distinction and not high, especially because the corpus considered three categories. Including +an at .50 weakens the manipulation.
issues.quote: These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50

issues.subcategory: Binary noun/adjective task ignores verb and other-category ambiguity
issues.description: Experiment 1 forces nonwords to be classified as nouns or adjectives, although some suffixes also occur in verbs or other categories and diagnosticity was computed across three categories. Forced binary responses may inflate apparent sensitivity and does not test full lexical-category knowledge.
issues.quote: participants indicated their adjective-noun decisions via button press.

issues.subcategory: Nonword stems not fully matched across suffix/category conditions
issues.description: The manuscript states stems were generated and concatenated with one suffix, but provides limited evidence that stems were matched across noun/adjective suffix conditions for phonotactics, bigram/trigram frequency, pronounceability, or semantic associations. Wuggy generation alone does not guarantee equivalence after suffix concatenation.
issues.quote: Eighty non-existing stems with a CVC structure were constructed using the Wuggy pseudoword generator... Each stem was concatenated with one suffix only.

issues.subcategory: Stimulus close-neighbor criterion vague
issues.description: The manuscript excludes 'close neighbours' and pseudohomophones but does not define the close-neighbor threshold or procedure, particularly for phonological neighbors in Experiment 2. This reduces replicability of stimulus selection.
issues.quote: we did not include any pseudohomophones (e.g. “sabal” – sable) or close neighbours of existing words

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 nonword appendix contains stimuli not listed in Experiment 1 appendix or spelling variants
issues.description: Experiment 3 claims experimental nonwords were selected from Experiment 1, but Appendix D includes items such as vudence whereas Appendix B lists nadence, ralence, sigence, and jofence. Some discrepancies may be typos, but they complicate replication and suggest inconsistency in stimulus reporting.
issues.quote: Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives (10 suffixes) or nouns (10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1.

issues.subcategory: Table 5 z value inconsistent with text
issues.description: The text reports regressions-out B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < .01, while Table 5 reports B = 0.25, z = 2.65. Both may be significant, but the inconsistency indicates reporting errors in model outputs.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction... (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: Table 5 go-past estimates inconsistent with text
issues.description: The go-past effect is reported as B = 41, t = 3.837 in the text and B = 43, t = 3.76 in Table 5. This discrepancy is small but indicates inconsistent reporting of statistical results.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.subcategory: No exact p values for many tests
issues.description: The manuscript often reports thresholded p values only (e.g., p < .0001, p > .5), reducing transparency and making it difficult to evaluate evidence strength, especially for exploratory and multiple tests.

issues.subcategory: No blinding where manual judgment is involved
issues.description: Manual extraction/coding of suffix spellings could be influenced by coder expectations if coders knew condition. The manuscript does not state whether coders were blind to congruency/context. This matters for subjective or ambiguous spellings.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings

issues.subcategory: Behavioral effects attributed to long-term knowledge without ruling out task strategies
issues.description: Especially in explicit classification and spelling tasks, participants may infer the experimental purpose or use overt suffix rules during the task. The manuscript interprets findings as long-term implicit knowledge but does not assess awareness or strategy use.
issues.quote: These results suggest that skilled readers’ long-term knowledge represents the statistical structure of the writing system.

issues.subcategory: Awareness and explicit strategy not measured
issues.description: No post-experiment questionnaire or debriefing is reported to determine whether participants noticed suffix-category contingencies or adopted explicit strategies. This is particularly important because Experiment 1 explicitly asks for lexical category judgments of suffix-bearing nonwords.
issues.quote: You will be asked to decide if a letter string looks like a noun or an adjective.

issues.subcategory: Skilled-reader claim not supported by objective reading measures
issues.description: Participants are assumed to be skilled readers based on undergraduate status and self-report of no difficulties. No standardized reading or spelling assessments are reported, limiting claims about skilled readers as a defined population.
issues.quote: They were native English speakers with no history of reading, spelling, or learning difficulties.

issues.subcategory: OSF link view-only but preregistration/data availability specifics not described
issues.description: The manuscript points to OSF storage but does not specify which files contain raw data, analysis scripts, processed data, exclusions, or whether the link is permanent/anonymized. Data availability is helpful but not a substitute for complete methodological reporting.
issues.quote: The OSF storage for this project (https://osf.io/hac5j/?view_only=52edb714e2624029be443c8dff7cb81d) contains stimuli, data, and analyses associated with the work reported in this article.

issues.subcategory: Typographical and bibliographic errors affecting precision
issues.description: There are several typos in references and text (e.g., 'Univeristy', 'Clair' missing 'St.', 'to understanding'), which are minor but reduce professionalism and can hinder reference retrieval.
issues.quote: Preliminary analyses we conducted to understanding why some morphemes are diagnostic, while others are not.
